messages.author: 21b39e2b255e81ed
messages.subject: convergence problem in a multi-level multivariate regression
parts:
I have a simple model looks like the following 
Basically, there are 281 variable and 151 observations where I would like to have some shrinkage like lasso (but preferably, non-parametric) and a multi-level variable next to it, each would like to get 3 different coefficient for each level.

I couldn't figure out to make it vectorize (specially the multi-level part) - but unfortunately have a convergence problem. Any recommendation ?

data {
     int<lower=1> Nobs; // number of subjects (151)
     int<lower=1> p; // number of taxa (281)
     int<lower=1> Ngroup; // number of taxa
     int<lower=1> group_id[Nobs]; //indicator variable for each observation
     vector[Nobs] y; //body weight
     vector[Nobs] x_pt; // previous bw matrix
     matrix[Nobs, p] X; // abundance matrix
     }

parameters {
  vector[Ngroup] alpha; // slop for each group
  vector<lower=0,upper=30>[Ngroup] etta; // intercept for each group
  vector<lower=0>[Ngroup] sigma; //error scale
  vector[p] beta;
  vector<lower=0>[p] hs_local; 
  real<lower=0> hs_global; 
}

model {
  hs_local ~ student_t(1, 0, 1); 
  hs_global ~ cauchy(0, 1); 
  beta ~ normal(0, hs_local * hs_global); 
  
  for (i in 1:Nobs){
    y[i] ~ normal(etta[group_id[i]] + x_pt[i]*alpha[group_id[i]] + X[i]*beta, sigma[group_id[i]]);
  }
}

messages.subject: Re: convergence problem in a multi-level multivariate regression
parts:
On Friday, September 30, 2016 at 8:58:24 PM UTC-4, Dana Robertson wrote:
I couldn't figure out to make it vectorize (specially the multi-level part) - but unfortunately have a convergence problem. Any recommendation ?

You pretty much have to use a non-centered parameterization for these hierarchical shrinkage priors in Stan and even then, you probably have to crank adapt_delta up to 0.99999... and then get lucky. There is some code for the non-centered parameterzations at

https://github.com/jpiironen/rstan-varsel

Ben

> y[i] ~ normal(etta[group_id[i]] + x_pt[i]*alpha[group_id[i]] + X[i]*beta, sigma[group_id[i]]);

y ~ normal(etta[group_id] + x_pt .* alpha[group_id] + X * beta, sigma[group_id]);

Why are you constraining intercept in (0, 30)? You can have sampling problems
if the value are near the boundaries, which will also bias estimates compared to
letting etta be unconstrained. If yo8u have a y that's constrained to be positive,
you can also log transform. Log weight might make more sense for modeling anyway.

student_t(1, 0, 1) and cauchy(0, 1) are the same distribution.

Plus, there's the scale identifiability issue Andrew pointed out in:
> beta ~ normal(0, hs_local * hs_global);

Those Cauchy priors are only very very weakly identifying hs_local and hs_global.

- Bob

Thanks for your comments,
In fact, your #1 suggestion made it much much faster and the convergence is much much better after incorporating https://github.com/jpiironen/rstan-varsel !! I didn't it is possible to vectorize an operation in stan as such.

1) Regarding the sparsity, posterior mean for coefficients are not exactly zero (as one could expect). I wonder, if picking the coefficients above a certain threshold is the only way or there is another smarter approach ?

2) I constrained the intercept in (0, 30) because I know it can not be larger than that !

3) What do you mean by log transform of y ? do you mean, log transferring the y beforehand ? or formulating it as
 log(y) ~ normal(etta[group_id] + x_pt .* alpha[group_id] + X * beta, sigma); 

I know my y has both lower and upper bound ! but I am not sure, how that can be incorporated 

Thanks again for your input, 

P.S here is the code, for future reference

functions {
// square root of a vector (elementwise)
vector sqrt_vec(vector x) {
vector[dims(x)[1]] res;

for (m in 1:dims(x)[1]){
res[m] <- sqrt(x[m]);
}
return res;

}
}


data {
     int<lower=1> Nobs; // number of subjects
int<lower=1> p; // number of taxa

int<lower=1> Ngroup; // number of taxa
     int<lower=1> group_id[Nobs]; //indicator variable for each observation
     vector[Nobs] y; //body weight
     vector[Nobs] x_pt; // previous bw matrix
     matrix[Nobs, p] X; // abundance matrix
     }

parameters {
  vector[Ngroup] alpha; // slop for each group

vector<lower=0>[Ngroup] etta; // intercept for each group
  real<lower=0> sigma; //error scale
  
  // auxiliary variables for the variance parameters
vector[p] z;
real<lower=0> r1_global;
real<lower=0> r2_global;
vector<lower=0>[p] r1_local;
vector<lower=0>[p] r2_local;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> tau;
vector<lower=0>[p] lambda;
  vector[p] beta;
tau <- r1_global * sqrt(r2_global);
lambda <- r1_local .* sqrt_vec(r2_local);
beta <- z .* lambda*tau;
}

model {
  y ~ normal(etta[group_id] + x_pt .* alpha[group_id] + X * beta, sigma); 
  z ~ normal(0, 1);
r1_local ~ normal(0.0, 1.0);
r2_local ~ inv_gamma(0.5*3.0, 0.5*3.0);
// half cauchy for tau
r1_global ~ normal(0.0, 1.0);
r2_global ~ inv_gamma(0.5, 0.5);
}

Where does this knowledge come from? If it's a prior, then
we'd suggest expressing it more softly on an unconstrained
parameter (or one that's positive-constrained if that's a physical
constraint of the system).

If it comes from the data as in you expect it to be close to the data mean,
which might be 15, then just let the data pull it there.
want it to emerge from the model's generative

If the upper bound of 30 is a physical constraint on some system, then
it should be baked in with constraints as part of the data generating
process being modeled.

- Bob
